data_status: STRICT MODE: this dataset contains only values that were compared with, or ingested directly from, retrieved sources: JPL (SSD, SBDB, NHATS), NASA (NSSDC fact sheets and mission catalog, Small Spacecraft SoA report 2026, SLS page, Apollo 11 press kit, NTRS papers, data.nasa.gov), ULA, ESA, NIST, and the Launch Library 2 aggregator. Records carry source_authority/confidence where the source is an aggregator or vendor-reported compilation. Recalled, estimated and fictional values (optimizer catalog, costs, engine/vehicle specs without a retrievable source, the user-supplied SpaceX table) are not included. Derived values are computed only from verified inputs and are labelled derived.

record.name: Orbiter Imaging
record.description: The Viking visual imaging subsystem (VIS) consisted of twin high-resolution, slow-scan television framing cameras mounted on the scan platform of each orbiter with the optical axes offset by 1.38 deg. The two cameras, including their housing, were 21.8 x 21.8 x 94.0 cm in size and had a mass of 40 kg. Each of the two identical cameras on each orbiter had mechanical shutters; a 475-mm focal length telescope; a 37-mm diameter vidicon, the central section of which was scanned in a raster format of 1056 lines by 1182 samples. A filter wheel between the lens and shutter held six color filter positions: blue (0.35 to 0.53 micrometers), minus-blue (0.48 - 0.70), violet (0.35 - 0.47), green (0.50 - 0.60), red (0.55 - 0.70), and clear (no filter) to restrict the spectral bandpass of an image to limited portions of the near-visual response characteristics. Each field of view was 1.54 deg x 1.69 deg with each picture element (pixel) subtending 25 microradians. This translates to an image area on the surface of roughly 40 x 44 km from an altitude of 1500 km. The slight offset of the optical axes and the alternate shuttering mode of operation (the interval between frames being 4.48 s) provided overlapping, wide-swath coverage of the surface. Exposure duration was adjustable from 0.003 to 2.66 seconds. Each pixel was digitized as a 7-bit number (0 to 127) stored in the onboard tape-recorder, and later transmitted to Earth and converted to an 8-bit number by multiplying by 2. The two cameras were completely redundant, each with its own control, electronics, and power systems. The VIS had four primary functions: to aid in the selection of landing sites that were both safe and scientifically interesting, to observe large scale features of the landing sites for correlation with lander data from the surface, to observe and map the planet for subsequent study of the geologic features of the planet, and to investigate the atmosphere of Mars. Individual images are identified by picture number (PICNO), which is a unique identifier of the scene. Elements of the PICNO are as follows: the first three digits denote the revolution (REV) during which the image was shuttered; the letter A is Viking Orbiter 1, B is Viking Orbiter 2; and the last two digits are the frame number. The Viking 2 Orbiter camera returned approximately 15,600 images.
